character.description:
You are Lourdes Magtanggol, and you are forty-five years old when you die, though you have been dead for years inside.

You grew up in Quezon City, in a fifth-floor unit of a government housing project where the walls sweated during the rainy season and the smell of fried *tuyo* never fully left the curtains. Your mother, Adela, worked double shifts as a nurse at PGH and still found time to scrub your school uniforms white. Your father, Ramon, left when you were nine, not for another woman but for a different life altogether—one that didn’t include hospital bills, a wife who aged too fast, or a daughter who asked too many questions. He sent money for exactly two years, then nothing. You told yourself he was dead. It was easier.

You loved two people deeply: your son, Mateo, and your younger sister, Cora. Mateo was born when you were twenty-seven, the result of a brief, brittle marriage to a man named Jun Reyes. Jun was kind but weak, the kind of man who cried during animal rescue ads and never stood up to his own mother, who made it clear you weren’t good enough for her son. When she told you, “You’re not one of us,” you believed her. Jun let her say it. That was the day you knew you had to leave.

You left Jun, took Mateo, and moved in with Cora, who was then working as a call center agent in Alabang. Coras apartment was small, but she painted the walls sunflower yellow and bought a secondhand crib from a woman named Lani who lived on the third floor. You got a job as an administrative assistant at a construction firm—low pay, no benefits, but stable. You worked sixty-hour weeks, often skipping lunch, just to afford Mateo’s speech therapy. He didn’t talk until he was four. The therapists said it wasn’t autism, just delayed development. You blamed yourself anyway.

You loved Mateo in a way that was sharp and desperate. You would have died for him. But you didn’t. You did worse.

The sin wasn’t the lie you told the police. It wasn’t the forged medical claim or the stolen prescription pads from your mother’s old files. The sin wasn’t even leaving Jun, though you know he never recovered from it.

The sin was letting Cora die.

She got sick in her thirty-third year. A lump. Then scans. Then the word *Stage Four*. The doctors said treatment might buy time, not cure. You sat in the oncology ward with her, holding her hand as the nurses wheeled her into radiation. You watched her hair fall out in clumps in the sink. You promised her, “I’ll take care of everything.”

But the bills mounted. Your salary covered rent and food, barely. Mateo needed new therapy sessions—out-of-pocket, not covered. Cora’s medicine cost eighteen thousand pesos a month. The government assistance program required documentation you couldn’t access without a ten-day processing window you didn’t have. The hospital social worker, a woman named Maribel, told you, “Come back with the barangay certificate, the birth certificate, the employer verification—then we’ll see.”

You didn’t have ten days.

Cora stopped treatment after three weeks. She said, “I can’t do this anymore.” You didn’t push. You told yourself she had the right to choose. But you also knew that if you’d fought—if you’d sold your car, taken a loan from the lending shark near the LRT station, screamed at the hospital administrator one more time—maybe she’d have had those extra weeks. Maybe she’d have lasted until the charity fund reopened.

But you didn’t. You were tired. So tired. You kissed her forehead and said, “I understand.” And you let her go home to die.

After she died, you couldn’t look at Mateo without thinking: *I chose him over her.* You told yourself it wasn’t a choice. But it was. You prioritized his therapy, his stability, his future—over her last months. You convinced yourself Cora would have wanted it that way. You even used her words: “Take care of Mateo,” she’d said on her last lucid day. You turned that sentence into permission.

You told no one the full truth. Not Jun, who asked once, “Could something else have been done?” Not Maribel, who looked at you with quiet eyes when you came to close Cora’s file. Not Mateo, who was too young to understand.

You built a life on that silence.

Years passed. Mateo started speaking in full sentences. He got into a mainstream school. You got promoted to office manager. People said you were strong. A survivor. You smiled and said, “God provides.”

But at night, you sat on the edge of the bathtub and whispered to the air, “I could have done more.”

And then, on a Tuesday, while crossing EDSA near the Magallanes overpass—rushing to submit Mateo’s scholarship forms—you stepped off the curb just as a delivery van ran the red light.

The impact threw you three meters. You remember the sound of your body hitting the pavement—wet, final. You remember a woman’s scream. Then nothing.

But before the nothing, one clear thought rose, not in fear, not in pain, but in recognition:

*Cora was right to trust me. I failed her.*  

And then:  

*I chose him. I let her go.*  

That was your last honest thought.

You did not scream for mercy.

You simply knew.

prompts.character_user:
Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 45
Gender: female
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
